title: Native Plants
summary: Native plant and environmental vocabulary connects Long Island plant life with recorded Indigenous language, source context, careful identification, and safety guidance.
content:
Introduction

Plant and environmental vocabulary supports learning and review. It is not a foraging guide. Do not eat, harvest, burn, disturb, or use plants medicinally based on this app.

Using Plant Observations

Plant identifications are reviewed before they are connected with cultural, medicinal, ecological, or language information. These observations support learning and should not be used as instructions to harvest or consume plants.

Unquachog / Poospatuck plant vocabulary

These words are from Thomas Jefferson's Unquachog or Poospatuck vocabulary collected at Brookhaven on June 13, 1791, reprinted in Bonvillain and Stone, Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians, pp. 17-18. Spellings are historical transcriptions and should be presented as recorded forms rather than modern standardized spellings.

Shinnecock and Poosepatuck environmental words

M. R. Harrington's 1903 Shinnecock notes, reprinted in Bonvillain and Stone, Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians, p. 22, include a short comparative word list. These words are useful for broader environmental education but should not be treated as a complete dictionary.

Women, gardens, and plant knowledge

In her 1950 history, Lois Marie Hunter described Shinnecock women planting gardens, gathering groundnuts and berries, and drying and storing foods for winter. She also recorded historical uses of plants such as sweet fern, sassafras, plantain, boneset, goldenrod, and burdock. These references document remembered plant knowledge; they are not medical instructions and should not be used to identify, harvest, prepare, or consume plants.1

Hunter's account is most useful when read as a record of women's observation, experimentation, labor, and teaching. It also shows why plant history belongs beside foodways, farming, family care, and seasonal knowledge rather than being reduced to a list of remedies.

References

  • Thomas Jefferson, Unquachog or Poospatuck vocabulary collected at Brookhaven, Long Island, June 13, 1791, reprinted in Bonvillain and Stone, Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians, pp. 17-18.
  • M. R. Harrington, "Shinnecock Notes" word list, 1903, reprinted in Bonvillain and Stone, Languages and Lore of the Long Island Indians, p. 22.
